quadHead: Four ways Egypt catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: Airport No-Meter Taxi
quad.tl: A man in an orange vest steers you past the rank to a curbside sedan quoting a flat 50 dollars to Zamalek — the metered fare is 150–250 EGP.

quad.title: The Philae Temple Boat
quad.tl: The posted Shellal crossing is 10 EGP; the boatman laughs at the sign and demands 500 EGP round-trip before he will take you to the Temple of Isis.

quad.title: Papyrus Factory Tour
quad.tl: A tea and a demo, then 5-dollar banana-leaf prints sell for 50 and 3-dollar fragrance oil pours into vials priced at 80 — your driver takes 30–50 percent.

quad.title: Fake Tourist Police
quad.tl: A man in khaki and a lanyard 'badge' walks you to a side desk by the Solar Boat Museum and demands a 30-dollar 'registration' fee that does not exist.

body: Egypt: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Egyptian Tourist-Police guidance (126), the Consumer Protection Agency (19588), r/Egypt threads and verified local reporting — researched from the source, not recycled from old blog lists.

43 specific scams across Cairo, Giza, Luxor, Aswan, Hurghada, Sharm El Sheikh, Alexandria and Dahab. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Arabic phrases that shut them down — with romanization and script you can show on your phone.
Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year, and the current edition sits in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Egypt relaxed, not braced.
